ABSTRACT Given the non-stationary, noisy, and regime-shifting nature of financial markets, constructing
robust alpha factor discovery engines that generalize out-of-sample while preserving economic inter-
pretability remains a critical open challenge. Standard Genetic Programming (GP) evolutionary algorithms
operate blindly on mathematical syntax without domain economic reasoning, frequently suffering from
semantic overfitting by selecting formulas that correlate with in-sample returns through structural noise
while being economically nonsensical. Prior LLM-augmented frameworks rely on structural tree pruning or
terminal rejection, resulting in severe formula attrition. We propose a novel regime-ensemble framework that
integrates a two-stage market regime factor engine with a post-evolution Two-Stage LLM Semantic Refiner.
In Stage 1, a locally deployed instruction-tuned model (Llama-3.2-3B) acts as an economic judge, scoring
symbolic expressions and gating only severely flawed expressions (S ≤ 2) for revision. In Stage 2, a domain-
constrained code mutator (Gemma-2-2B) performs deterministic semantic repair under a closed vocabulary
of valid financial features and operators, compiling candidate trees back into the evaluation loop. Evaluated
on a 23-year panel of Indian Equities (NSE Nifty 50, 2002–2025), the proposed framework elevates out-
of-sample annualized net returns from the 8.41% quantitative ceiling to 9.61% (deterministic peak) and
10.63% (heuristic peak), improving net Sharpe from 0.5518 to 0.6365–0.6465. Crucially, the architecture
substantially mitigates out-of-sample performance degradation, compressing Sharpe decay on the US S&P
500 from −35.03% (Vanilla GP) and −20.71% (HMM-GP) down to −6.77%, and halving degradation on
Chinese Equities (SSE) from −92.08% to −46.68%. This confirms that conditional LLM semantic repair
fundamentally prunes overfitted historical noise across diverse international asset classes.

However, standard GP suffers from a critical vulnerability:

(e.g., Information Coefficient or ICIR) over historical train-

Recent attempts to incorporate Large Language Models
(LLMs) into symbolic factor mining have followed two pri-
mary paradigms:
1) Structural Tree Pruning: Frameworks such as
TEDE [12] utilize LLMs to identify and prune over-

strictly syntactic and does not address the underlying
economic fallacy of an expression.

phaAgent [11] evaluate whether an alpha formula
aligns with macroeconomic hypotheses and outright
discard any candidate that fails semantic validation.

mentum with normalized volatility may be logically sound

primitive.

dynamics into persistent latent states, routing market

tion engines.

B. REGIME DETECTION AND SWITCHING MODELS
Financial asset returns are governed by non-stationary, state-
dependent stochastic processes characterized by fat tails,
time-varying volatility clusters, and abrupt macroeconomic
structural breaks [15]. Consequently, static single-state pre-
dictive models suffer severe performance degradation dur-
ing regime transitions. Markov regime-switching autoregres-
sive frameworks, pioneered by Hamilton [16], and Gaussian
Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) [17] have become foun-
dational tools for modeling latent financial states. Empiri-
cal studies have demonstrated that market dynamics across
distinct volatility and liquidity regimes exhibit fundamen-
tally opposing factor premia [18]–[20]. For instance, price
momentum factors that generate superior risk-adjusted al-
pha in sustained bull markets frequently suffer catastrophic
momentum crashes during sudden market inflection points,
whereas mean-reversion and value factors dominate during
high-volatility corrective regimes.
While regime-switching models have been widely applied
to top-down asset allocation and macroeconomic risk budget-
ing, prevailing quantitative methodologies treat factor genera-
tion and regime detection as entirely disjoint processes. Stan-
dard alpha mining engines optimize global factor expressions
across historical windows spanning multiple regime shifts,
forcing candidate expressions to average over contradictory
economic dynamics. By contrast, conditioning the symbolic
genetic programming search engine directly on latent HMM
states enables the evolution of regime-specialized alpha ex-
pressions tailored to the specific statistical properties of bull
and bear environments.

A critical yet under-addressed vulnerability in empiri-

driven by structural noise overfitting. As documented by

D. SENTIMENT-FUNDAMENTAL FUSION
An increasingly vital frontier in quantitative asset manage-
ment is the multi-frequency fusion of unstructured text senti-
ment with structured market prices and low-frequency fun-
damental metrics [31], [32]. Financial markets process in-
formation across heterogeneous temporal horizons: macroe-
conomic news and geopolitical announcements generate in-
stantaneous high-frequency sentiment shocks, daily OHLCV
bars record price discovery and liquidity flows, and quarterly
balance sheet filings reflect slow-moving enterprise valuation
and accounting health.
Deep multimodal neural networks can model complex non-
linear interactions across these disparate data streams, but
their black-box opacity, vulnerability to distribution shifts,
and susceptibility to adversarial text perturbations severely
hinder institutional adoption. The Adaptive Fusion Model
(FinALFA) [33] addresses this challenge by establishing an
interpretable macro fusion mechanism that dynamically com-
putes scalar mixing parameters to balance sector-standardized
fundamental ratios against FinBERT-derived news sentiment.
Integrating this macro sentiment-fundamental signal as a su-
pervisory conditioning layer provides a persistent macroeco-
nomic anchor that prevents genetic programming from over-
indexing on transient market microstructure noise.

consensus scoring (Llama-3B and Qwen-3B), and scaling to

VI. CONCLUSION
This paper introduced a quantitative factor discovery frame-
work fusing an Adaptive Fusion Model (AFM), Hidden
Markov Model (HMM), and Genetic Programming (GP) with
a Two-Stage LLM Semantic Refiner. Across a 23-year panel
of Indian Equities (Nifty 50, 2002–2025), the framework
elevated out-of-sample annualized net returns from the 8.41%
quantitative baseline to 9.61% deterministic / 10.63% peak
return (Sharpe 0.6365–0.6465). Crucially, the refiner sub-
stantially mitigated out-of-sample performance degradation,
compressing degradation on the US S&P 500 to -6.77%
and halving degradation on Chinese Equities (−46.68%). Fu-
ture research directions include domain-specific LoRA fine-
tuning of Gemma-2B on quantitative formulas, multi-agent
consensus scoring (Llama-3B and Qwen-3B), and scaling to
broad-market universes (NSE 500, Russell 2000).
